analysis.one_liner: Lets federal health regulators order immediate mandatory recalls of unsafe FDA-regulated products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2009 with no cosponsors and died in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Secretary of Health and Human Services the power to order companies to immediately stop making and selling any FDA-regulated product found dangerous, to warn people who used it, and to recall it from store shelves and medicine cabinets. Companies could contest the order at a hearing within ten days, and ignoring an order would be a federal crime under existing drug and food law. It also required a study and new rules on making voluntary and mandatory recalls work better.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use drugs, medical devices, food, and other FDA-regulated products. Today the FDA generally has to rely on companies to recall dangerous products voluntarily; this bill would let regulators compel an immediate stop-sale, public notice, and recall when a company will not act. Anyone exposed to a risky product would learn of the danger sooner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of FDA-regulated drugs and devices

how_it_helps.text: Gives the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to order manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers to immediately cease distribution, manufacture, and sale of a dangerous FDA-regulated product, notify people at risk, and implement an immediate recall.
Requires a prompt informal hearing within ten days, with the order staying in effect while the company's challenge is decided, and requires the order to be vacated if the grounds prove inadequate.
Makes failure to obey a recall order a prohibited act under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, enforceable through existing civil and criminal penalties.

Directs the Secretary to study recall effectiveness with manufacturers, distributors, retailers, public health groups, and consumer groups, report to Congress within 180 days, and issue implementing regulations.

analysis.who_pays: Drug, medical device, food, and other FDA-regulated product companies, which would bear the cost of immediate stop-sale orders, public warnings, and recalls, including lost sales on products later cleared at a hearing. Companies would lose the practical leverage of negotiating the pace and scope of a voluntary recall.

drawbacks.text: An order takes effect immediately and stays in effect while the company awaits its hearing, so a company that is later vindicated still loses sales and bears recall costs in the meantime.
The burden falls unevenly on smaller manufacturers and retailers, who have less capacity to absorb a sudden halt to sales and a nationwide recall.
The bill gives the Secretary broad discretion over what 'necessitates' a mandatory recall, with the main check being an informal hearing rather than advance review of the decision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is speed versus certainty: consumers learn about dangerous products faster, while companies face recall costs before any hearing can vindicate them. The ten-day hearing and the requirement to vacate unsupported orders address the main fairness objection, and the enforcement penalty makes the power real rather than advisory. The main design question is how the Secretary decides when a recall is 'necessary' — the bill leaves that standard broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no action.

narrative.text: Rep. Betty Sutton introduced the bill on February 3, 2009.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 111th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug, medical device, and food companies avoided a mandatory federal recall authority and the stop-sale costs that come with it. Consumers gained nothing; the voluntary recall system the bill sought to tighten stayed as it was.

for.name: Rep. Betty Sutton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 3, 2009; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 3, 2009 and never reported the bill out.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health (Energy and Commerce)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 4, 2009 and held no hearing or markup on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one besides the sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never showed itself.

industries.note: The bill would let regulators force an immediate stop-sale and recall of a dangerous drug without waiting for the company's agreement, and make defiance a federal offense. Companies lose control over the timing and scope of recalls, while consumers get faster warnings.

industries.industry: Medical device and FDA-regulated product manufacturers
industries.note: The recall authority covers any FDA-regulated product, so device makers and other regulated manufacturers would face compelled recalls, public risk notices, and lost sales on products later cleared at a hearing.

industries.industry: Distributors, importers, and retailers of FDA-regulated goods
industries.note: They would be directly bound by recall orders, adding compliance costs and inventory losses. But a faster, more credible recall system protects retailers from selling dangerous products to their customers.
